meta.title: Where do you lean? — experiential learning cycle
meta.description: A short reflection tool used before the CISV Facilitating Learning session. Nothing you enter leaves your device.

intro.title: Where do you lean?
intro.lead: {n} sets of four statements. Rank each set. At the end you will see which part of the experiential learning cycle you leaned towards today — or that you leaned towards two, or none clearly — and where to stand in the circle when the session starts.
intro.privacyTitle: Nothing you enter leaves this device
privacy: There is no account, no server and no database. The whole thing runs in your browser.
Nothing is uploaded, and nothing is sent anywhere — not while you answer, and not when you finish.
No cookies, no analytics, no third-party requests. Even the fonts are served from here.
If you want to keep your result you press a button and it is written into the web address, which stays on your device. Nobody collects it.
intro.whatTitle: What this is, and what it is not
what: It is a way of noticing that a room of trainers contains four different appetites, and that a facilitator has to run all four.
It is **not** a psychometric test, not a diagnosis, and not a label. It has never been validated.
Research does not support choosing training methods to match a measured learning style. The [about page]({aboutHref}) says what that means and what this would have to do to claim otherwise.

assessment.instruction: Rank these four from 1 to 4. 1 is the one most like you, 4 the one least like you. Each number is used once. Think of what you usually do, not what you should do.
assessment.announceSwapped: Rank {rank} given to: {statement}. {other} moved to rank {otherRank}.
assessment.announceDisplaced: Rank {rank} given to: {statement}. {other} is no longer ranked.
assessment.announceComplete: All four ranked. You can go to the next set.
assessment.incomplete: Rank all four statements to continue.
assessment.leaveWarning: Your answers are only held in this page. If you reload, you start again.

result.title: Where you leaned today
result.disclaimer: This is a preference, not a diagnosis. Research does not support choosing training methods to match someone's measured style. We use this so you can see that a group contains all four appetites, and that a trainer needs to run the whole cycle — not to tell you how you should be taught.
result.leanPoint: Across the {n} sets you ranked the **{name}** statements above the others by a clear margin: {lead} points ahead of the next.
result.leanBetween: Two neighbouring parts of the cycle came out ahead of the other two, close to each other: **{first}** and **{second}**.
result.leanOpposite: Two opposite parts of the cycle came out ahead of the other two, close to each other: **{first}** and **{second}**.
result.leanSpread: No part of the cycle came out clearly ahead today. Your first choices changed from situation to situation. That is a result, not a failure to answer.
result.standPoint: When the session starts, stand at the **{name}** point, {where}.
result.standBetween: When the session starts, stand on the circle halfway between **{first}** and **{second}**. The trainer may ask you to join one of those two groups.
result.standOpposite: When the session starts, stand in the centre of the circle, on the line between **{first}** and **{second}**. The trainer may ask you to join one of those two groups.
result.standSpread: When the session starts, stand in the centre of the circle. The trainer may ask you to join a group that is short of people.
result.lowest: You ranked the **{name}** statements lowest, {gap} points below the next. Is that the part of the cycle you are most likely to skip when you plan a session?
result.margin: Differences of less than {tau} points are inside this quiz's margin: answering on another day could easily reverse them. A clear result rarely moves to a different part of the cycle on another day, but it often moves to a neighbouring position.
result.circleTitle: The learning cycle, with your scores and where to stand
result.circleDesc: The learning cycle drawn as a circle, running clockwise: Active at the top, Reflective on the right, Theorist at the bottom, Pragmatist on the left. The shape inside shows your four scores, further out for a higher score; the dashed ring is the middle. The marker shows where to stand.
result.shapeLead: Each score runs from {min} (always ranked last) to {max} (always ranked first); {mid} is the middle. The four always add up to {total}, so a high score in one place means lower scores elsewhere.
result.tableCaption: Points for each part of the cycle
result.tensionsLead: Kolb describes the cycle as two pulls: between experiencing and conceptualising (top and bottom of the circle), and between reflecting and experimenting (right and left). These compare only the two opposite parts, so they can differ from your overall lean.
result.saveLead: Your result is already in this page's web address, after the # sign. That part is never sent to any server. Bookmark it, screenshot it, or print it.
result.copyFailed: Could not copy — select the address bar and copy it by hand.
result.staleTitle: This result was made with an earlier version
result.staleVersion: This link was made with version {saved} of the quiz, which used a different model and different statements. Its result cannot be shown in the new form. Answer the {n} sets again to get a result.
result.revisedVersion: This link was made with version {saved} of the statements; these are version {current}. The parts of the cycle and the scoring are the same, so the result below is still yours — but some of the wording has changed since.
result.badLinkTitle: That link could not be read
result.badLink: The result in this address is damaged or was made by a newer version of this tool. Nothing was lost — the answers were never stored anywhere else, so the only way forward is to answer again.

about.title: About this instrument
about.who: This was built for CISV International's *Facilitating Learning* session, part of Train the Trainer. That session asks trainees to arrive knowing which part of the experiential learning cycle they gravitate to, stand at that point of a circle on the floor, and talk in those groups. The assessment it used to link to is dead, and the replacements were either unlicensed copies of commercial instruments or available only in English. This is one CISV can own, in more than one language.
about.what: {n} sets of four statements, each ranked from 1 (most like you) to 4 (least like you). A first place is worth 4 points and a fourth place 1, added up for each part of the cycle, so each scores between {min} and {max} and the four always total {total}. Because you rank rather than rate, the scores compare your own preferences with each other; they say nothing about how strong a preference is compared with other people. The result names one part of the cycle only when it is at least {tau} points ahead of the next. Smaller differences are within the margin a quiz of this length can see, and the result then puts you between two parts or in the centre.
about.model: Kolb's experiential learning cycle has four stages, which he calls learning modes: concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation and active experimentation. Honey and Mumford later linked one learning preference to each stage. This quiz uses that stage-by-stage reading: Active (experiencing) at the top of the circle, Reflective (reflecting) on the right, Theorist (conceptualising) at the bottom and Pragmatist (experimenting) on the left, in the order the cycle runs. Note that Kolb's 'active experimentation' is the Pragmatist point, not the Active one.
about.notValidated: This is a reflection tool. It has no psychometric validation of any kind: no reliability data, no test–retest data, no factor analysis, no norms, no pilot. Nobody has ever answered it under conditions that would let anyone say what it measures.
about.whatWouldItTakeTitle: What would have to be true before it could claim otherwise
whatWouldItTake: Every statement understood as intended in both languages, checked in think-aloud interviews and by trainers who sort the statements into the four parts of the cycle without seeing the names.
The four statements in each set about equally attractive, so that no part of the cycle wins or loses because its statements sound better.

Scores that hold up when the same people answer again two to three weeks later: a correlation of at least .70 for each of the four scores, and fewer than 1 in 20 clear results moving to a different part of the cycle.
All of this checked separately in English and in Portuguese, because a translated questionnaire is a new questionnaire.
about.whyNotAlpha: Two checks often quoted for questionnaires, Cronbach's alpha and factor analysis, do not work on ranked answers like these, because everyone's four scores add up to the same total.
about.evidence: Learning-styles research is clear on one point: there is little evidence that teaching people in the style they prefer helps them learn more. A 2024 meta-analysis found a small average advantage for matched teaching, but the pattern the idea depends on appeared in only about a quarter of the outcomes, and its authors conclude that the benefit does not justify the effort. The session uses the cycle differently: as a reminder to plan learning that moves through all four parts, rather than only through the part a trainer enjoys. That is a planning idea, not a measured effect, and this tool claims no more than that.
citations: Pashler, H., McDaniel, M., Rohrer, D., & Bjork, R. (2008). Learning styles: Concepts and evidence. *Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 9*(3), 105–119. [doi:10.1111/j.1539-6053.2009.01038.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1539-6053.2009.01038.x) — set out what a fair test of matching would have to show and found almost no studies that passed it.

Coffield, F., Moseley, D., Hall, E., & Ecclestone, K. (2004). *Learning styles and pedagogy in post-16 learning: A systematic and critical review.* Learning and Skills Research Centre. — identified 71 models and evaluated 13 influential ones in depth, finding persistent problems with reliability and validity, including in Kolb's inventory.

Clinton-Lisell, V., & Litzinger, C. (2024). Is it really a neuromyth? A meta-analysis of the learning styles matching hypothesis. *Frontiers in Psychology, 15*, 1428732. [doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2024.1428732](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2024.1428732) — small average effect; the required crossover in about a quarter of outcomes.

Kolb, A. Y., & Kolb, D. A. (2017). Experiential learning theory as a guide for experiential educators in higher education. *Experiential Learning & Teaching in Higher Education, 1*(1), article 7. — the cycle as a guide for designing learning.
about.soWhatTitle: So why run it at all
about.soWhat: Because the session is not about you. It is about a room noticing that it contains four different appetites, and that a trainer who only runs the part they enjoy will lose three quarters of the room. Getting people to stand in different places and argue about it does that. A measurement would not do it better.
about.ip: The statements were written for this tool from descriptions of the four stages of the cycle. None is taken or adapted from Honey and Mumford's Learning Styles Questionnaire, Kolb's Learning Style Inventory or KELP, the Honey–Alonso CHAEA or the Felder–Soloman ILS. The Portuguese names match those used for the CHAEA in Brazil, but this is not the CHAEA, and its scores cannot be compared with any of those instruments.
about.privacy: No backend, no accounts, no analytics, no cookies, no third-party requests. Everything is computed in your browser and nothing is transmitted. Saving a result writes it into the part of the web address after the # sign, which browsers never send to a server. There is no way for a facilitator, or for us, to collect results: a facilitator sees your result because you show it to them.
